text: A fabric merchant's wife in 1940 Japan begins to notice that her husband's absences have a shape, and decides to find out what it is. Kurosawa builds the thriller out of domestic materials: rooms, meals, the tone two married people take when one of them is withholding. The war the country is arguing itself into reaches Satoko secondhand, as rumor and inference; it stays a marriage first. What keeps the film taut is that she does not remain the person things happen to. She conceals her own intentions as carefully as they are concealed from her, and the suspense becomes a matter of endurance: how long can a household hold when both halves of it are running a private calculation. Venice gave the direction its Silver Lion, and Kinema Junpo named it the best film of its year.

The assignment is seduction, and seduction takes time, so the film spends all one hundred and fifty-eight of its minutes taking it. Shanghai under the Japanese puppet government is a city where everyone performs loyalty to somebody, and the young woman sent to get close to a collaborating official does her work the way an actress does: in costume, in company, in rooms where the talk is about nothing. Venice gave it the Golden Lion and Taipei its Golden Horse for best feature. None of that is a promise of comfort. Ang Lee stays patient to the point of discomfort about what sustained pretending costs the one doing it, and denies her the protection spy films usually extend to their agents: any distance at all from the man she is deceiving.

One letter, addressed to three women at once, announces that its writer has gone away with one of their husbands and declines to say whose. The withheld name is the design: three marriages, one suspicion, and a day in which each wife can do nothing but reconsider what she believed she understood. There is no crime in it. A sentence in a letter does the work of one. Mankiewicz, who wrote it as well as directed it, took the Academy's awards for both jobs and the Directors Guild's for the second, and the method he was rewarded for is conversation: the wives' own accounts of how each match was made, what it cost, who has been keeping score. The film's cruelty is that none of them can ask the one question outright.

A circus can be reformed only as far as its audience will follow, and the young woman who inherits one here means to find where that line falls. She takes over from a father who worked the trapeze, and takes on with it a set of ideas about what a circus might be instead. Kluge keeps the balance sheet visible: what a change of program costs, who pays for it, what the crowd bought a ticket to see. Ambition and receipts are the two quantities here, and they do not reconcile. Television, when she turns to it, is not a defeat so much as the same problem in a larger room, where an audience still has to be reached before it can be altered. Venice gave it the Golden Lion, the German Film Award for best feature followed, and it holds a place on Die wichtigsten deutschen Filme.

One hundred and eighty-eight minutes, two dozen Los Angeles lives, and nobody at the center of them. Altman took Raymond Carver's stories, small and flat and exact about what people fail to say, and let them share a city, so that a waitress who hits a boy with her car in one strand passes through another as a stranger, and an uncollected birthday cake becomes a campaign of harassment. Venice gave it the Golden Lion and it holds a place on They Shoot Pictures Don't They? 1,000 Greatest Films, but the interesting part is structural: proximity is the only thing connecting these people, and proximity turns out to be enough to do real damage. The comedy is constant and it is not kind, and the cruelty in it is mostly the ordinary kind, produced by inattention rather than malice.

Country music has always been able to state damage plainly, and the film borrows that plainness for a man who has stopped explaining himself. Mac Sledge sang once and drank more; the picture picks him up after the collapse rather than during it, which spares us the scenes everyone expects and leaves the harder ones. A young widow and her son take him on as company. The Academy honored the man playing Sledge and the original screenplay, which took the Writers Guild award as well, though the writing's method is mostly subtraction: ninety-two minutes, few explanations, no scene in which anyone accounts for a life. His career resumes. The film treats that as an ordinary consequence of being useful to someone, which is a rarer idea than it sounds.

An empire that has stopped believing in itself still needs officers who believe, and Alfred Redl makes a career out of supplying exactly that. Szabó spends most of 152 minutes on the climb: the accent adjusted, the origins edited, the friendships chosen for what they open. Austria sent it to the Academy Awards, and the German Film Award for best feature followed. The army in it rewards a man for becoming unlike himself and keeps a record of the change; Redl's destination is the Secret Police, an office whose business is other people's secrets, which is an uncomfortable posting for someone carrying several of his own. Political deception closes in there. The film is less curious about what he betrays than about how much of himself he had already spent buying the uniform.

A woman is on trial for killing her lover, and the film's real subject is the jurors, each of whom hears the evidence through a life the court knows nothing about. Cayatte cared about the machinery rather than the crime. The same testimony reaches each of them and comes back out as a different story, every version sincere, every version bent by a marriage, a bereavement, a grudge carried in from outside the building. Nothing depends on a hidden clue. What accumulates instead is a quiet case against the assumption that ordinary people, given facts, will produce anything but their own biographies, and the film is careful not to propose a better system in its place. It holds both the Golden Bear and the Golden Lion, a strange weight of festival regard for a picture that consists largely of people arguing in a small room.

Three generations of shipbuilders live under one roof, and a fourth is born while the yard that feeds all of them is being reorganized. The Zhurbins are a hereditary trade: grandfather Matvei, his son Ilya, and Ilya's sons Aleksei, Anton and Viktor, whose quarrels take place in the same rooms where the work is discussed. The film puts household and shipyard on one footing. A change of method at the yard becomes a change in what a father can teach a son, and the heaviest trials fall to Aleksei, the youngest, at the point where the family's craft stops being the right thing to have inherited. What carries the hundred minutes is the texture of a crowded house: meals, arrivals, the long practice of people who cannot get away from each other.

The question at the center is whether a family should leave the only street its children have ever known. Branagh keeps the camera at Buddy's height, so the trouble outside arrives as it would for a boy: adults lowering their voices, streets that stop being neutral ground, games that end early. Buddy's own life stays largely intact inside the crisis, with school and jokes and a first romance, and the film, which took a People's Choice Award and the Academy's award for its original screenplay, is warmer toward the household than it is curious about the politics pressing on it. That is a limit and also a choice. What it gets right is the negotiation between two parents doing arithmetic they would rather their son did not overhear.

Told from the height of a boy who is not frightened enough, wartime London turns into something closer to an unsupervised summer. The frame is a grown man remembering, which lets the film hold both the memory and the correction to it: what an air raid meant to a child, what a ruined house offered him, what the adults were carrying that he registered but could not read. Boorman keeps the scale domestic, one street and one family and one school, and lets the war be weather that other people worry about. The Golden Globes classified it as a comedy and were not wrong. Los Angeles critics gave it their best-picture award, and the British Film Institute later placed it on its list of a hundred British films. It is funny the specific way families become funny about danger in retrospect.

The border here is a frozen river, and a car will cross it if the ice holds and the driver has decided she has run out of better options. Ray Eddy needs a down payment on a home; her husband has taken the money and gone. Lila, a widowed Mohawk woman who knows the route and the jurisdictions it crosses, needs the work as badly. Hunt shoots the smuggling as labor: cold, repetitive, badly paid. Sundance gave her first feature its grand jury prize and New York critics called it the year's best first film, and the reason shows in how the tension is built, out of thin ice and gas money and what is in the trunk rather than out of pursuit. The two women never soften into friends. They stay partners, which is harder and more particular.

A psychoanalyst spends his working days absorbing other people's pain, and it turns out to be no preparation for his own. Moretti builds the early stretch out of household nothing: meals, errands, the small negotiations of a family that likes each other. That is the investment. When the ground gives way, the film has already established exactly what is at stake in it, and the professional detail turns cruel, since a man whose job is explaining feeling to strangers must go on sitting in the room with people who pay him to do it. Cannes gave it the Palme d'Or and Italy its David di Donatello for best film. Nothing in it is raised to the pitch of tragedy. The register stays domestic, and the film trusts that a household described this closely will be recognized without anyone underlining it.

Ron Kovic enlisted out of conviction, came home paralyzed, and spent the years afterward turning the distance between those two facts into a political life. The Academy gave Stone its award for direction and the Directors Guild agreed. He tells it at full volume across 145 minutes, and the volume is part of the argument: a boyhood of parades and promises, then a war, then a ward, then a man learning to say in public what he was raised not to say. Irony is not available to the film and is not attempted. The film treats belief as the injured thing. The patriotism came first and was sincere, which is why the sense of betrayal costs so much, and why the activism reads as continuous with the enlistment rather than a reversal of it.
